articles.title: How Raising Cane's Became an A-List Magnet
articles.summary: Celebs from Adrien Brody to Teyana Taylor and Matthew Rhys are flocking to parties thrown by the chicken tender chain’s charismatic CEO.
articles.content:
There's a new billionaire in town — and this one's ready to party.

Todd Graves, founder and CEO of chicken fingers chain Raising Cane's, has quickly gained a reputation for hosting Hollywood's hottest events, splashing out for A-list gatherings around major sporting events and awards shows.

During last summer's World Cup, the 54-year-old Louisiana native rented out stadium suites nationwide, throwing parties with guests including Woody Harrelson , Sacha Baron Cohen, Mick Jagger, Halle Berry , Jamie Foxx, Ashton Kutcher, Adam Brody, Florence Pugh, Alix Earle , Tate McRae and Matt Damon (during opening weekend of The Odyssey , no less). He also enlisted Tiffany Haddish to serve chicken fingers and host Raising Cane's-branded interviews backstage at the Emmys, persuaded Adrien Brody to paint a custom mural for his Times Square store and is getting the biggest winners across sports and awards season to come by his restaurants immediately after their victories, establishing a tradition to rival the post-awards In-N-Out run. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return Movies Teyana Taylor Sells Female-Driven Comedy to Warner Bros. (Exclusive)

How exactly did a brand serving $15 chicken finger meals — whose nearest competitor is Chick-fil-A — become such a popular collab magnet for the rich and famous? Graves says the secret sauce is his own up-by-the-bootstraps backstory, which he sees as the ultimate icebreaker: Having worked as a boilermaker in California oil refineries and as a salmon fisherman as a young man, he went on to launch his fast food empire — which 30 years later, according to Forbes , has landed him a net worth of $20 billion.

Graves says he does not pay celebrities to attend his events but instead provides a high-end, all-inclusive outing. "I want it to be like, 'I want to go hang out with Todd and go to this event.' It's first-class, great hotels, transportation, security," Graves says of his pitch. "No one in there wants anything from them but friendship, hanging out." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He adds that on top of the fact that “the dinners are great, the parties are fun, there's DJs and performers that they like,” it’s important to him to take out the corporate element, with no business partners in his rooms “hitting people up or asking for selfies.”

There is a catch: Graves does ask his guests to post on their social media channels, telling them up front that " 'It helps me get a return on this and we can keep doing great events,' and they're all cool about doing that." Haddish and Snoop Dogg have been particularly enthusiastic posters for the brand, while on the Raising Cane's channel, Tom Brady declared its Fanatics Fest event (which featured a dunk tank of Cane's sauce) "my favorite part of the entire week."

Graves confirms that the company measures impressions after every event, and "it's amazing for sales," he adds. "You see long-term loyalty because [customers] are like, 'The person that I really love and respect loves Cane's and actually wants to hang out with the founder.' "

The CEO, who this year bought a home in the Hollywood Hills for a reported $23 million, says he doesn't do cold calls to invite people he doesn't know. "It looks like a branded thing," he says, which, to be fair, it very much is, judging by the ubiquity of the chain's logo in celebrities' posts. Instead, he fills his events with stars with whom he is friendly. That helps him expand the Hollywood circle in a more organic way, through word-of-mouth. Damon, for instance, came to the Raising Cane's World Cup celebrations because Casey Affleck, a friend of Graves', vouched that the events were good. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Graves' friend group also includes Adrien Brody — who showed off his artwork while Graves was hanging out at the actor's home, leading to the idea to paint a custom piece for the New York store — and Teyana Taylor , who dropped by a Cane's for a photo op after winning at the Golden Globes earlier this year. "We want to be part of culture when it happens," he says, having organized the plan with Taylor before the awards show, getting her to come by before her night of parties. (These photo moments are executed as more traditional brand deals.)

The Raising Cane's founder says he was on the road 260 days in 2025, and he doesn't seem to be slowing down as the brand expands into Europe and begins to plan international events. (Baron Cohen is helping connect him to contacts in London, Graves says.) He also notes that despite his connections and financial status, he doesn’t have any aspirations to produce projects or be actively involved in Hollywood — though he does think another friend, Leonardo DiCaprio, should play him in the story of his life.

But L.A. remains as much of a home base as Louisiana. "The town has so accepted me. [It's] so diverse, so rich culturally. I love it," Graves says. "So for me, [the goal] is just to keep meeting these great people. L.A. is so full of all these amazing people that I get inspired by."

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6's Satire Is More Important Than Ever, and I Hope Rockstar Never Loses Its Bite
articles.summary: Courtesy of Rockstar Games At some point, the Grand Theft Auto series is going to have a serious problem: reality is getting very good at doing its job. Why bother inventing a deranged internet celebrity when you can open your phone and find someone livestreaming a public meltdown for an audience of millions? Why write a ridiculous conspiracy theory […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google At some point, the Grand Theft Auto series is going to have a serious problem: reality is getting very good at doing its job. Why bother inventing a deranged internet celebrity when you can open your phone and find someone livestreaming a public meltdown for an audience of millions? Why write a ridiculous conspiracy theory when there's probably already a podcast dedicated to it, complete with a merch store and a suspiciously expensive subscription tier? And why dream up some absurd fictional advertisement when the real world seems determined to make every product sound like it was conceived during a fever dream? These days, society is practically writing the jokes for it.

Still, there is no reason for Grand Theft Auto 6 to hold back. Quite the opposite, actually. Now that the long-awaited sequel has finally arrived, Rockstar has an opportunity to deliver some of the sharpest satire the series has ever seen. The franchise has never been particularly interested in treating modern culture with reverence, and that's a huge part of why I've always found it intriguing. Beneath the explosions and criminal escapades, there's a cynical sense of humor that makes whatever its talking about absurdly close to the reality its pulling from. Its both hilarious and sad, yet I desperately want the studio to paint something completely unhinged on it, to mirror the way the world really run. The last thing I want is a Grand Theft Auto that suddenly remembers its manners.

The funniest thing about making a modern Grand Theft Auto game might be that Rockstar barely has to exaggerate some of the things it wants to mock anymore. Think about the internet personality who will do practically anything for a few seconds of attention, for example. These people don't need to be particularly convincing as fictional characters anymore because the real versions are already out there, running amok, creating the content Rockstar needs. All Rockstar has to do is turn the dial until the absurdity becomes impossible to ignore.

GTA 6 has brought players back to Vice City, but the world surrounding it feels unmistakably shaped by the internet age. Its public presentation has already introduced social-media personalities and the sort of internet-fueled characters who could comfortably spend an entire day arguing with strangers online. Imagine driving through Vice City and having the entire world feel like one enormous algorithmically generated circus. That's pretty much real life these days, and that's the kind of environmental storytelling the series does so well.

There's another reason I'm so protective of Grand Theft Auto 's sense of humor: the series has never been at its most interesting when it's trying to make everyone comfortable. Its satire works because it doesn't politely ask permission before making a joke. In a lot of ways, its kind of of like South Park . Sometimes it's absurd. Sometimes it's downright mean. Occasionally, it lands on something so uncomfortably familiar that the laughter takes a second to arrive. That's part of the appeal. A good joke doesn't necessarily need to make its target happy, and I would hate to see Rockstar become so concerned with avoiding controversy that it sands away the personality that made the franchise distinctive in the first place.

That doesn't mean I want GTA 6 to chase outrage or mistake being offensive for being clever. There's a really big difference between having something interesting to say and simply trying to provoke a reaction. Rockstar is at its best when it understands the ridiculousness of the world it's parodying, then finds a way to make that ridiculousness even more ridiculous. Grand Theft Auto, as franchise, as pretty much always been controversial because many don't what the series it poking fun at. It has always been more than a crime simulator with a wicked sense of humor. It's a funhouse mirror pointed directly at society. If society wasn't so ridiculous in itself, there'd be hardly anything to write satire about. But, because that's the not case, I hope Rockstar has absolutely no intention of straightening GTA 6 or any other future titles, out, because that would just be boring. You've just gotta laugh at life's perpetual insanity, and Rockstar understand this well.

What parts of modern culture do you think GTA 6 does best at satirizing, and where do you want Rockstar to push its humor even further? Let us know in the comments below.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It looks like Emily Blunt is finally ready to dive back into the world of this cult-classic action film that first made its theatrical debut back in 2015. The actor recently sat down with Kyle Buchanan on The Kyle Buchanan Show , where they discussed whether she had a burning desire to return to the world Denis Villeneuve brought to life when he directed Sicario over a decade ago . The answer in short? "Not really," said Blunt, well, bluntly.

“I think it was something… look, when we made the film and then when it became what it did…I don’t think it did great when it came out. It did okay. And then it became this cult-classic,” she went on to elaborate. Blunt and Buchanan went on to dissect the film's cult status, and the hopes that bringing back the original cast would be able to tap into those same vibes, despite this threequel being on the franchise's third director ; Padraic McKinley ( The Weight ) is stepping into the director's chair for this one, while Stefano Sollima was at the helm for the second Sicario film, which focused solely on Benicio del Toro's Alejandro and Josh Brolin's Matt.

Emily Blunt came on TKBS for a totally charming conversation that also happened to tease SICARIO 3. Link in comments! pic.twitter.com/COlPyhFC0J

When asked about the reception of the film in recent years and her experience with fans, Blunt said, "Oh, it’s amazing. So I think it just—it’s funny, every time I go through passport control, they’re like, ‘I love Sicario .’ Anytime I meet anyone in Special Forces, security, passport control, the police, they love it. It had such a life force to it. And so they went and did the second one, and I was not written into that one, so I was like… but then I think they just feel that there’s a third act to play, and I love that world, and I love those guys.”

It's true that Blunt's Kate Macer didn't appear in Sicario: Day of the Soldado , but it seems she's more than ready to reunite the cast for a third run. It'll be very interesting to see where Macer is now, as the first movie followed the FBI agent as she became involved in a harrowing mission that put her up against drug cartels along the border between the U.S. and Mexico. "We're gonna have to see," was all Blunt said when asked how idealistic Macer would be a decade after the events of the first film.

The franchise's third installment is said to be headed in an entirely new creative direction, with Padraic McKinley and Steven Knight ( Peaky Blinders ) running the show. Narrative details are being closely guarded, but it's safe to say that both the danger and the drama will be full tilt, with the entire original cast coming back together

articles.title: Batman: Year One Changed the Dark Knight Forever, but 40 Years Later, It's Time for Something New
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics Origins are an essential part of superhero stories. Given that comic book heroes are designed to star in never-ending stories, they need strong, defined starting points from which all future stories can draw inspiration. Status quo is king, after all, so origins need to serve as a thesis statement for how these characters develop into […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Origins are an essential part of superhero stories. Given that comic book heroes are designed to star in never-ending stories, they need strong, defined starting points from which all future stories can draw inspiration. Status quo is king, after all, so origins need to serve as a thesis statement for how these characters develop into who they are. Importantly, they also need to be adaptable. Given that heroes tend not to age, they typically exist on a sliding timescale, meaning that their earliest years are repeatedly moved up in time to be closer to the present day. Every few years, origin stories tend to be reimagined and updated. All except for "Year One."

Batman's "Year One" is often cited as not just his definitive origin, but one of his greatest stories put to page . It modernized Bruce Wayne's journey from trained warrior to Batman, even adding Jim Gordon's arrival and rise in Gotham. It was a foundational tale about their partnership, and it's been treated as his definitive origin ever since, even superseeding the New 52's "Zero Year." However, it was only meant to serve as his post- Crisis reintroduction, not as his singular starting point. Every other popular hero has had their origin retold at least once by this point, so today, we're examining exactly what made "Year One" work so well, and why it still might be time for a new version.

Before diving into why we need a new story to supersede "Year One," let's talk about why it's stuck around for so long. For starters, it provided the foundation for the modern interpretation of Batman while simultaneously being vague enough in characterization to make practically any interpretation of the character work. Batman is presented as a brooding but inherently kind man, who strives to help as much as he does to inflict vengeance. It leans into every part of Batman's character like balancing on a tightrope. Beyond that, it's incredibly well-written, knowing exactly what to focus on to build the mythos, reimagining past scenes with a gravitas and seriousness that helped cement Batman as someone important.

I could rave about "Year One" all day, but suffice to say, it's a perfect starting ground for Batman because it's a short, contained story that tells you everything you need to know about how he operated in his early years and how his partnership with Gordon started. Any fan could read it in an afternoon and dive into any other modern Batman comic with at least a decent understanding of who Batman is. It's timeless yet feels distinctly grounded in its own time, which both helps sell it but also is exactly the reason that this comic needs to be reworked for the current timeline. It is, after all, a snapshot of Batman's fights against the gangsters and mobsters who ruled Gotham's underground . Just take a look at this trailer for the animated adaptation.

The point being, "Year One" has aged as well as any story could hope to, but it's simply time for new origins to explain how Batman fits into the modern DC mythos, which has significantly changed since the immediate aftermath of Crisis on Infinite Earths . DC has fully embraced its fantastic and strange roots that it tried so hard to shy away from when "Year One" released. The story it provides no longer completely reflects the DC around Batman. The question of continuity and history is constantly changing, but DC is making a substantial effort to tie its heroes to a timeline. It's no mistake that Superman's history as Superboy is being expanded on at the same time Wonder Woman received a rework of her own origin, both of which bring in modern sensibilities and smooth their ages.

Continuity has always been a messy thing in comic books, but with DC's decision to embrace its entire history and characters' overlapping lives following Dark Nights: Death Metal , it's become more essential than ever to specify what's canon and not. Batman has usually shirked this problem, with the New 52 citing that the vast majority of his famous stories took place on a hyper-condensed time scale, but with things more convoluted than ever and it having been decades since a lasting update to his first outing as Batman, there are more than enough reasons to warrant a new take on this classic tale.

A modern version of Batman's origin would definitely draw heavily on "Year One," but it would also likely steer away from the militaristic outlook that Bruce had. Given that Batman is essential in the second wave of superheroes rising in DC, it's likely that major villains and other heroes wouldn't have a presence. Still, why it would almost certainly focus on the corruption in Gotham City, with the Justice Society of America and Superboy returned to continuity, it would probably also involve the rise of the costumed supervillain as much as the old mafia that had a death grip on Gotham.

Most likely, we'd see a three-way battle between the corrupt powers-that-be like Falcone, an ambitious up-and-coming gangster-type villain like Penguin or the Ventriloquist, and the forming duo of Batman and Gordon. Importantly, a new origin for the Dark Knight would need to embrace the less grounded aspects of his character, presenting Batman as something more than a detective who wears a funny hat. It has to feel distinctly superheroic, which is one of the things that, while present in "Year One," always felt somewhat on the back burner. We need to see Batman as a superhero in his origin, instead of just blossoming into one or being a good man with great skills.

At the end of the day, Batman's origin is still one of DC's greatest, and while it's about time to relay the groundwork, "Year One" will always be a classic Batman tale. What change would you make to Batman's origin, if you could make just one? Let us know in the comments below!

Andrew Rannells recently revealed that Kevin Spacey asked him out while the “Girls” actor was starring in “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway.

“I’ve never told this story before. He asked me on a date once,” Rannells said while guesting on “The Downside” podcast hosted by Gianmarco Soresi. “He sent me a letter to ‘The Book of Mormon.’ Handwritten.” The actors went on to explain that the Oscar winner came to see the musical and “came backstage” to meet him after the show. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Creators Pounce on Midterm Elections, Hoping to Win New Viewers and More Dollars Emma Chamberlain, Wesley Wang, Aryna Sabalenka and More Unveil New Projects for YouTube

“There were always a lot of really fun people there, but sometimes they would bring them up into our dressing rooms, but with no notice,” he said. “So after the show, we’re getting changed. There’s a knock on my door. It was Goldie Hawn, Kevin Spacey, and Joel Schumacher. They were not together, but they all walked up together. So then we were all crammed in my dressing room.”

Rannells continued: “Kevin Spacey was sort of rubbing my neck as we were standing there… Joel Schumacher, who was very close to me, he said, ‘Stay away from that man.’” That prompted Spacey to respond, “Hey! C’mon, c’mon,” he recalled. “And then like a week later, I got a handwritten letter from him asking me on a date.” Rannells concluded by noting he “never responded” to the note.

Rannells originated the role of Elder Price in the long-running musical, performing from the show’s opening in 2011 through June 2012. The part earned him a Tony nomination for best leading actor in a musical.

Spacey’s sexual assault allegations came years later in 2017, when fellow Broadway actor Anthony Rapp said that the actor assaulted him in his New York apartment while Rapp was a teenager. Rapp later filed a $40 million civil lawsuit for sexual assault and battery in 2022, but a New York jury found Spacey not liable on all counts. Earlier this year, Spacey reached a settlement with three men who sued him over sexual assault claims, avoiding a civil trial in London that was set for October.

articles.title: Journalist Shared One Normal Person Tidbit About Timothèe Chalamet After Interview Went Viral (In Awkward Way)
articles.summary: Stars are just like us.
articles.content:
Given he's one of the world's biggest stars, Timothée Chalamet's life remains a topic of curiosity . Of course, as a star's fame rises, it's not unheard for them to reveal less about themselves. On that note, when Vanity Fair editor Mark Guiducci was given the task of profiling the megastar, he had a bigger task than he initially thought. The interview has now gone viral for awkward reasons, but Guiducci is defending his work and sharing a complimentary note about Chalamet.

However, this turned out not to be the case. Chalamet remained incredibly guarded and opted out of talking about his life. He declined to answer questions or comment on his high profile relationship with Kylie Jenner (with the latter admittedly being something he's long opted not to discuss). He did however spend a lot of time making observations about Guiducci’s home decor, which ended up becoming the centerpiece of the article. As a result, the story has gone viral due to Chalamet's evasive, awkward nature as well as the piece feeling more like it's about Guiducci’s apartment rather than Chalamet.

Considering Chalamet grew up in New York City himself and still spends a lot of time in the Big Apple , he’s likely used to drinking New York’s tap water. Plus, I wouldn't be surprised if he had some sort of awareness that if he asked for anything specific it would end up in the article. I personally don’t doubt that Chalamet was kind, charming, and easy going, especially since the Dune star has been described as being “normal” before. It’s just hard to get a true read on a person when the person in question is aware they’re being observed.

articles.title: As A Theater Kid, I Have So Many Feelings About Elsinore
articles.summary: Andrew Scott's drama hit me where I live.
articles.content:
Actor Andrew Scott is synonymous with playing Hot Priest in Fleabag (streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription ), but he's a versatile star of the screen and stage. Those two worlds combine in the new LGBTQ+ movie Elsinore , directed by Simone Stone. The biographical drama film tells the story of late actor Ian Charleson, who performed the title role of Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly struggling with AIDS in the midst of the AIDS crisis. The movie is endlessly powerful, and I have so many thoughts as someone who comes from the theatre.

While Club Kid is my favorite movie of the year (so far) , Elsinore is another LGBTQ+ story that I feel privileged to have seen. The movie tells the real-life story of Ian Charleson struggling with AIDS while also preparing to play the behemoth role of Hamlet at the National Theatre. It's a truly gut-wrenching story, told expertly through the film's 111-minute runtime. Throughout the movie, I was shook by how seen I felt by the way it portrayed working on a theater production.

Then there was the process of line memorization. Ian is shown drilling lines pretty much non-stop throughout Elsinore , including when he's getting treatments and even while recovering after being hospitalized. This rings so true to me; if I'm in a dialogue-heavy play, I function in the same way. For instance, when I played Prior Walter in Tony Kushner's Angels in America, I couldn't stop drilling my lines. That includes testing myself with flashcards, as well as repeating my monologues every time I was in the shower and/or driving in the car.

articles.title: Critically Panned 2016 Movies That Are Actually Worth Watching 10 Years Later
articles.summary: It’s easy to get nostalgic about 2016, especially when you realize that was 10 whole years ago. Beyond being the final year of “millennial optimism,” it was also a fantastic year for film lovers. Masterpieces like Barry Jenkins’s Moonlight, Denis Villenueve’s Arrival, and Damien Chazelle’s La La Land graced our screens, while even disappointments like […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It’s easy to get nostalgic about 2016, especially when you realize that was 10 whole years ago. Beyond being the final year of “millennial optimism,” it was also a fantastic year for film lovers. Masterpieces like Barry Jenkins’s Moonlight , Denis Villenueve’s Arrival , and Damien Chazelle’s La La Land graced our screens, while even disappointments like Jared Leto’s Joker in Suicide Squad became hilarious fodder for internet memes—back when the internet was still fun.

However, if you look past the best and worst movies of 2016, you’ll find a plethora of films that were critically panned at the time but still have a lot of merit. One is a classic case of so bad it's good. A few are misunderstood masterpieces from filmmakers unfairly considered past their prime. And another is a brilliant early work from a filmmaking duo who hadn’t quite reached their peak yet. Regardless of the reason, this handful of 2016 films, while hated by critics when they came out, are absolutely worth watching today.

A psychological horror thriller from Drive director Nicolas Winding Refn , The Neon Demon holds a “Rotten” score on Rotten Tomatoes and was slammed for being all style and no substance. Critics at the time weren’t necessarily wrong about the film prioritizing its glossy visuals, but many failed to appreciate that, here, the style is the substance. On rewatch, it becomes clear that the arguably shallow characters and stilted, artificial dialogue were deliberate choices meant to mirror the vapid culture of the Los Angeles modeling scene the film is directly critiquing. 

Elle Fanning's fantastic lead performance is reminiscent of Naomi Watts in Mulholland Drive and shows the protagonist’s transformation from a bright-eyed, bushy-tailed dreamer into a narcissist. Natasha Braier's cinematography makes every frame look like a high-fashion editorial, while Cliff Martinez’s electronic score drives the tension. It may read as surface-level satire on first watch, but the film has retained some devoted fans for good reason.

The most objectively hated film on this list is Kevin Smith’s 2016 horror-comedy Yoga Hosers , which currently holds 26% on Rotten Tomatoes, although legend says it had 0% when it first came out. The main issues plaguing it are a messy screenplay, a home-movie structure, and low-effort practical effects. Yet despite the initial negativity, the film has developed a niche following, driven mostly by the chemistry between stars Lily-Rose Depp and Harley Quinn Smith, not to mention the B-movie camp. 

The plot follows two yoga-loving 15-year-olds working at a convenience store, but when an ancient evil awakens beneath the shop and threatens their plans to attend a party, they use yoga to battle an army of mini Nazi bratwursts known as the Bratzis. The absurdity is exactly why this film is worth a watch. It is by no means a “good” movie, but it’s so bad and so bizarre that it ends up being entertaining, fitting squarely into the “so bad it’s good” category. Alongside the two teen stars, Johnny Depp reprises his role as an eccentric French Canadian manhunter. The rest of the cast is equally stacked, featuring Justin Long as a yoga guru and Austin Butler as the party host, plus Natasha Lyonne, Haley Joel Osment, Vanessa Paradis, and a famous cameo from Stan Lee . At only 88 minutes long, the film is worth watching today if you love camp, B-horror, or teen-girl action flicks.

Written and directed by legendary filmmaker Terrence Malick, shot by three-time Academy Award winner Emmanuel Lubezki, and starring Hollywood A-lister Christian Bale, Knight of Cups was teed up to be a masterpiece. However, the film, about a disillusioned Hollywood screenwriter seeing a spiritual breakthrough, currently holds a 47% critics’ rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Reviewers cited a lack of any narrative structure and so-called self-indulgence from Malick, who inserts his own perspective into the story with little subtlety, as reasons for the hate.

Yet, while it might not live up to the profundity of Malick’s masterpieces like The Tree of Life , it’s still worth a watch for anyone who enjoys his sensibilities as a filmmaker. The stunning wide-angle cinematography is captivating enough to lead you through the story’s allegory of modern alienation, which uses tarot archetypes. Alongside Bale, the cast features Cate Blanchett as his ex-wife, Natalie Portman as his married lover, and supporting roles from Brian Dennehy, Antonio Banderas, and Imogen Poots, with voice narration by Ben Kingsley.  For a film initially dismissed as hollow, there’s actually much to glean from its spiritual pilgrimage. 

Swiss Army Man was the directorial debut of Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, also known as the Daniels, who would later go on to helm the Academy Award-winning Everything Everywhere All at Once . But before they were Oscar darlings, their early A24 film Swiss Army Man polarized critics and audiences alike, triggering notorious walkouts at its festival premiere and barely earning a “Fresh” score on Rotten Tomatoes. Today, it seems to have transcended the label of cult favorite, becoming known in cinephile circles as something of an unsung masterpiece.

The premise follows Hank (Paul Dano), stranded on a remote island and on the verge of suicide, when he spots a corpse washed up on the shore. He names the body Manny (Daniel Radcliffe) and discovers it possesses strange, Swiss Army knife-like abilities. At the time, it was famously known as “the farting corpse movie,” with detractors criticizing the juvenile humor, pretentious “twee” vibe, and moral greyness involving Mary Elizabeth Winstead’s character. Yet, for audience members willing to embrace the foolishness, Swiss Army Man is a rewarding watch. Rather than using shock value for cynicism, the Daniels use bodily functions as a metaphor for shame, stripping Manny of social conditioning as the film probes themes like depression, anxiety, and social masking. Without Swiss Army Man , there would be no Everything Everywhere All at Once . To understand the creative DNA that led the Daniels to their masterpiece, you must see Swiss Army Man .

What critically panned 2016 movie do you still defend? Let us know in the comments below.

articles.title: Ice Age: Boiling Point Brings the Hit Franchise Back to Theaters After 11 Years - Watch New Trailer
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of 20th Century Studios Ice Age is coming back to theaters with the sixth major entry in its franchise, and the first new theatrical release for the movies in over a decade. Ice Age has been dormant for the past few years following the release of its The Ice Age Adventures of Buck Wild spinoff with Disney+ a few […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Ice Age is coming back to theaters with the sixth major entry in its franchise, and the first new theatrical release for the movies in over a decade. Ice Age has been dormant for the past few years following the release of its The Ice Age Adventures of Buck Wild spinoff with Disney+ a few years ago, and most of that is due to the fact that original owners Blue Sky Studios have since shuttered their doors amid the move over to 20th Century Animation and Disney.

Ice Age had been rumbling about coming back with a new feature film entry for the last few years , and this was finally confirmed to be the case last year with the reveal of Ice Age: Boiling Point. Coming to theaters next year after an 11 year long drought for the film franchise in theaters, the first full trailer for Ice Age: Boiling Point has given fans the first look at the new movie in motion with its returning voice stars. You can check out the trailer below.

Ice Age: Boiling Point is currently scheduled to release in theaters on February 5th next year , and is the first major entry in the franchise to not be produced by the now closed Blue Sky Studios. The Ice Age Adventures of Buck Wild director John C. Donkin returned to direct this new entry with franchise producer Lori Forte producing. It's also set to feature the majority of the voice cast from the previous films as well with some new additions to the fold as the big family continues to expand.

Ice Age: Boiling Point will feature the returning voice cast of Ray Romano as Manny, John Leguizamo as Sid, Denis Leary as Diego, Queen Latifah as Ellie, and Simon Pegg as Buck. Other returning members of the voice cast now confirmed include Josh Peck as Eddie, Chris Wedge as Scrat, and Adam DeVine as Julian. New additions to the voice ( including recastings for older characters ) include Coco Jones as Peaches, Ashley Park as Zee, Vincent Tong as Crash, Kari Wahlgren as Baby Scrat, Dee Bradley Baker as Jurassic Scrat, Eduardo Franco as Body, and James Austin Johnson as Clarence the Sprout Master.

Ice Age: Boiling Point is picking up where the franchise last left off as the Ice Age is continuing to warm up, and leading Manny and his family to wild new locations they have never seen before. Unfortunately by the looks of things this new feature doesn't seem to be on the same scale as the previous films' adventures to this point , and that might be even more noticeable when it makes its way to the big screen next year. But that's something that remains to be seen with audiences around the world.

Ice Age is only one of the many long dormant film franchises coming back to screen s with a new entry after many years, and that makes it all the more compelling for what we can expect to see next year. But how are you feeling about Ice Age: Boiling Point so far? Let us know all of your thoughts about it in the comments.

articles.title: This GTA VI Comparison To Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour Blew My Mind (But Fans Are Less Impressed)
articles.summary: In both cases, it'd been a long time coming.
articles.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI came out on November 19, and literally one day after that, it was announced that it had hit $3.79 billion in sales. That’s a seriously impressive number. I mean, it took Taylor Swift nearly two years to make $2 billion with her highly profitable Eras Tour . GTA did more than that in one day. However, while that is quite mind-blowing to think about, fans aren’t so impressed by this comparison.

To get into the specifics, it was reported by Rockstar Games that GTA VI has reached $3.79 billion in sales as of November 20, per The AP . It also stated that 32.5 million units were sold in pre-release. When People published a story on what the video game had reportedly made, it prominently noted that it had already outgrossed Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.

Looking at the Eras Tour, specifically, after its 21-month run, it racked up $2 billion in tickets sold and over 10 million people attended the concerts (its proshot was also a major box office success and can now be streamed with a Disney+ subscription ). The NYT , that’s “double the gross ticket sales of any other concert tour in history.” Also, reportedly, the tour’s average gross per night was between $14 and $17 million.

When you really think about it, comparing GTA to the Eras Tour is like comparing apples and oranges. One is a concert tour; the other is a video game. Yes, they’re both major moments of monoculture. However, that’s kind of all they have in common. So, that left people commenting things like this on People’s post about the video game outgrossing Swift’s tour:

Something many comments pointed out was that there was a cap on how many people could attend the Eras Tour. There are only so many people you can fit in a stadium. Anyone can buy and play Grand Theft Auto VI . So, it makes sense that it could make more than the tour in such a short period of time.

articles.title: Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes
articles.summary: The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year's top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023. But female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for […]
articles.content:
The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year's top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023.

But female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for their music. Laura Karpman, composer of "American Fiction" and the current Netflix miniseries "East of Eden," has entered her first film as director in the documentary short subject category: " Cosmic Symphony ." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘GTA 6’: First Half-Hour Reveals Major Plot Twist Rockstar Has Managed to Keep Secret for Years 'GTA 6' Earns Rave Reviews and Lands 99 Metacritic Score, Tying for Highest-Rated Game of All Time

The film is a timely look at four musical artists who lost priceless, beloved instruments in the Palisades and Eaton fires of January 2025: composer Starr Parodi, whose 1928 Steinway piano was heard in dozens of MGM scores including "The Wizard of Oz"; songwriter Diane Warren, who lost a Yamaha grand; jazz bassist John Clayton, whose string bass was nearly 200 years old; and Altadena educator Susie Chung, whose brown Steinway was played by Lady Gaga in "A Star Is Born" and on the 2019 Oscarcast.

"I believe my piano has a soul… I have a little regret that I left her alone," Chung says in the film, and that sentiment is echoed by the other musicians. "Instruments have hearts, they have souls, they have lives," says Warren, a 17-time best song nominee. Two days before the fires, Warren was filmed performing her Oscar-nominated song "The Journey" on the piano in her Malibu beach house.

Clayton's bass, once owned by the legendary Ray Brown, had accompanied Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole and Duke Ellington. Recalling its past, he said "that bass and the music that it made was bigger than any of us could ever be." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Parodi describes her lost keyboard as having "this beautiful, haunting, bell-like sound… warm and thick," and she tells the harrowing story of watching her house go up in flames via their doorbell camera and later unearthing the remains of her MGM piano in the rubble.

Thousands of instruments were reduced to ash during the L.A. fires. "I felt it was a story that was really important to be told," Karpman says. "When you live with these instruments, they have personalities, they see history."

In addition to the interviews and performance footage, she added lively, colorful animation to the story. Animator Tempe Hale sought "to make the instruments come alive again, (to convey) the kind of fun and glory and energy that these instruments have."

Karpman also composed the score for her film, incorporating both orchestral and choral sounds to suggest the music still being made, in the beyond, by those lost music makers.

Scottish composer Anna Meredith wrote one of the year's most unusual scores for the romantic fantasy " Wicker ," which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her artificial husband, made for her by a basket weaver in their medieval village.

The entire score is played by just four people: a violist, a cellist, a recorder player and Meredith herself. "I'd much rather start small with a tiny lens, and see what you can do with it, rather than have every sound in the world, where it could just sound like any old thing. You have to really think creatively," she says.

Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson reached out to Meredith during shooting (to write music for a wedding scene), and she quickly became part of a team that included several women in key roles (including editor Sofi Marshall). The composer decided that the timeframe and the nature of the story demanded wooden instruments for a "timeless quality."

Meredith used as many as 10 different recorders, "from tiny little baby ones, only 20 centimeters; lots of ones in the conventional treble tenor range; and some bonkers instruments, including a bass one and a contrabass one which was so tall we had to move to a different recording studio. We had to find one with a skylight to fit the neck of that one, like seven feet tall." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The recorders represented the fisherwoman and her wicker husband, while the strings (the darker sounds of viola and cello) represented the villagers. "It's not nice string sounds," she says, "it's slithery, nasty sounds. Their sound worlds are, initially, kept quite different, and then the strings sort of ‘infect' the recorders as the villagers start to impose on their relationship."

The directors "wanted the score to be bold," Meredith adds, "and it's loud as well. The music is upfront. I'm very proud to be part of a film with a strong female story and so many important female elements, both on and off the screen, that have been part of it."

For " Tenzing ," the untold story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who accompanied Edmund Hillary to the top of Mount Everest in 1953, Norwegian-born, Stockholm-based composer Rebekka Karijord insisted on cultural authenticity. "I felt, early on, that we needed to have a collaboration with Nepalese musicians that isn't like an exotic tone or a color," she says. "It had to be a deep collaboration."

She enlisted a Nepalese spiritual leader and Buddhist nun, Ani Choying Drolma, to contribute traditional Buddhist chants; Nepal's premier flautist and throat singer Manose Singh; and actress Thinley Lhamo, who plays Tenzing's wife Dawa in the film and is also a highly regarded singer of Tibetan opera.

Lhamo "has the most amazing voice," Karijord says. That voice becomes, in a sense, the sound of the mountain itself. "I wanted to have something that could transcend the physical effort, that could pull us into the spiritual aspect, and her voice really solved that for me throughout the score."

In addition, she had the sound team record a number of unique sounds from the region—yak bells, goat bells, the sound of prayer wheels in the temples, Tibetan singing bowls and gongs—which she and her percussionist sampled and added to her musical library for incorporation into the score.

The film details England's drive to be the first nation to reach the summit of the world's tallest peak, Karijord points out. "It needed the big cinematic muscles, a meeting between Western and Eastern. If I could make the mountain, this goddess, beautiful and pristine and dangerous and magnetizing, then we will understand why're drawn to her—both Tenzing as a little boy growing up at the foot of the mountain, and these Englishmen wanting to conquer it." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Karijord employed a 40-piece string section from the London Contemporary Orchestra, in part to convey the danger of crevasses, avalanches and rumbles in the ice, along with a handful of woodwind and brass players and a 12-voice choir. Textural elements, such as the sound of breathing, also became a factor in the score.

Regarding the few female composers scoring studio films, Karijord notes that "it's such a deeply empathetic craft to score films, and it's a deeply collaborative craft. I know a lot of women who are both very empathetic and collaborative and brave. So I think there should be more of us doing it."

articles.title: How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories
articles.summary: For years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI. Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications. “It seemed to have […]
articles.content: For years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI. Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications. “It seemed to have real contempt for mankind,” Rich says. “It scared the hell out of me.” Rich published a book, “which was completely ignored,” and found himself striking out in his attempts to get attention with magazine articles. “So, in desperation,” he recalls, “I was like, ‘Maybe if I got a movie star…’” He got Andrew Garfield. In “ Artificial ,” Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a blithely destructive sociopath who manipulates his way into the center of a potentially civilization-ending technological advance. Rich uses the juicy character to tell a story about the most consequential political issue of the present moment. “I’ve been living with knowledge of this danger for at least five years, due to my fluke friendship with this scientist,” he says. (Selsam issued a public warning about AI’s increasingly uncontrollable behavior in September.) “I wrote this film out of a desperation to communicate to the world this information.” That desperation may be unique to Rich. But the desire to use the tools of screenwriting to illuminate political concerns is certainly not. Had “Artificial” simply been an enumeration of AI’s dangers, it’d likely have attracted as much attention as Rich’s book; instead, it’s a well-told story with a sharp argument at its core. That makes it one of several movies this year that use character and incident — the stuff of quality storytelling — to illuminate their writers’ very real political concerns. That goes for the year’s most-discussed blockbusters: Writer-director Christopher Nolan has imbued “The Odyssey” with a rueful sense of what it means to lose one’s humanity in wartime, while, if it’s anything like its two predecessor films, “Dune: Part Three,” written by Denis Villeneuve and Brian K. Vaughan, promises to examine the uses, and misuses, of power. But it’s showing up across more human-scale dramas this fall, as well. Take “ I Play Rocky .” The film depicts the writing and production of “Rocky,” which — before it was an Oscar-winning smash — was the Hail Mary attempt of unknown actor Sylvester Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) to write himself a place in the industry. For screenwriter Peter Gamble, the story has resonances well beyond Hollywood history. “‘Rocky’ came out right after the Vietnam War, and it was a time when people needed to believe,” Gamble says. Stallone, in the film’s telling, is the ultimate underdog; Gamble, who himself yearned for a screenwriting breakout, could relate. The message of the film, the writer says, is intended in part for his children: “They’re like, ‘We’re all going to die from global warming. If not, AI is going to kill us next week.’ What power do I have in the universe at all? We need to believe in ourselves again.” American history provides many stories that feel akin to the charged atmosphere of recent years: One, as Gamble notes, is the demoralization of the Vietnam War, and another is the cataclysm of the Great Depression. “ The Weight ,” written by Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, is a rip-roaring adventure film in which unjustly imprisoned convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) has the chance to win his freedom by transporting gold bricks across an unruly wilderness. The viewer roots for Murphy in part because he’s compellingly played by a movie star, and in part because the boot under which he struggles looks, at a moment of increased attention to mass incarceration and wealth inequality, familiar. “You don’t want it to be didactic and message-y or preachy in any way,” Gaines says. “But the idea was to try and tell a good story on a personal, individual level and hope that it would echo sympathetically with things that happen on a larger social level — both during the Great Depression and today.” Murphy’s journey depicts the stakes of its historical moment in frankly personal terms — his loss of freedom means the loss of access to his daughter, a crisis the film treats with gravity and righteous anger. “Abstraction doesn’t help you as a writer much,” Gaines says. “If you want to convey something, the heart is the place to start.” Or you can go for the gut. “ Ink ,” which James Graham adapted from his own stage play, makes the case that Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) created the venal media world we live in today. The dawning realization that Lamb, especially, is a force for evil hits particularly hard because Graham has, in the film’s early going, taken pains to make him so charming and his exploits so rootable. “You need these people to surprise you,” Graham says, “so that you want to be in that newsroom — and suddenly, weirdly, for a brief moment, you might even want them to get one over on the establishment.” How did tabloid culture gain such purchase? Because, as the film’s characters make clear, we’re willing to pay for it. “ Being Heumann ” makes us root for its band of rebels, too — but, in this case, they’re working to bring about a better world. The biopic, written by Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig, tells the story of Judith Heumann (Ruth Madeley), the activist who led the 1977 demonstration over the government’s failure to enforce disability-rights legislation. By its nature, the film is explicitly political, but its screenplay is also the product of a thoughtful, careful approach to representation and inclusivity. Taussig, who, like the late Heumann, uses a wheelchair, saw a certain power in learning about — and then writing about — the many activists Heumann helped organize. “What was so exciting about the research,” she says, “was this gold mine of learning about these absolutely compelling people.” The first-time screenwriter had grown up seeing “very little disability representation — and [when there was], it always felt so flat. There is a richness to the experience of disability that gets missed if you don’t live it and you can’t portray it.” Taussig’s ability to mine her own insights enriches the film, one that Heder, an Oscar-winner for “CODA,” intended to inspire and delight audiences, as well as educate them. “It’s very important to me that this story reach the widest audience possible,” Heder says, “because the events of the story actually were about a triumph. In a time where a lot of us are feeling really helpless, it was so important to express disabled joy and humor. I wanted to take the audience on a really entertaining ride, where they could leave seeing the world differently.” “Fjord” has a similar reframing effect — though its true-life basis is substantially more downbeat than Judith Heumann’s story. Cristian Mungiu took inspiration from the story of the Bodnariu family, an immigrant couple whose five children were taken away by the Norwegian state amid accusations of child abuse. “Fjord” presents the story of Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) in a who-do-you-believe social drama, one with painful repercussions. “What I’m looking into, in the stories that I pick up,” Mungiu says, “is this possibility of speaking about something bigger than just that story.” For its writer-director, “Fjord” addresses the painful consequences of globalization, as people from different traditions find that they cannot in fact understand one another. “It’s not a reenactment” of the Bodnariu story, he says: “That’s the starting point of a story in which everything is structured to speak about the relationship between the majority and the individual.” “Fjord” won the top prize at this year’s Cannes; the runner-up, “Minotaur,” also places a family drama in counterpoint with a story of major import. Here, a story of marital infidelity (based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film “The Unfaithful Wife”) plays out in 2022 as Russia is scaling up its military actions against Ukraine. Writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev had been working to put the film together for years — and, as he wrote, the mobilization against Ukraine was all over the news. “It was a very logical thing,” he says through a translator. “I started to fill gaps in the script with the realities of what was happening.” Like Simon Rich trying to spread the word against AI, Zvyagintsev used his script to convey what he was hearing, like local mayors asking businesspeople to choose which of their employees will be conscripted. “This is not something I took from the air,” Zvyagintsev says. “This is real information that came by phone. People would be afraid to speak up about those situations.” For Zvyagintsev, this use of character to explore the world around him is what screenwriting is all about. “The whole ocean,” he says, “can be reflected in one ocean drop.” Related Stories ‘GTA 6’ Upsets Conservatives: Fox News Tells Fans to ‘Grow Up’ as Clavicular and More Manosphere Influencers Complain About Lucia 'GTA 6' Presales 'Far in Excess' of Expectations Ahead of Next Week's Launch, Take-Two CEO Says

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google One of the major creators from Shueisha's Weekly Shonen Jump magazine has already come back with a new series only a year after their previous work came to an end. Shonen Jump is now at its final transition of the year as some of the longer projects are coming to an end, and new manga titles are set to kick off their respective serializations. What's been interesting for this batch in particular has been the fact that these new titles are actually from experienced creators .

Mission: Yozakura Family originally ended its run with Shonen Jump last year after six years of serialization , and series creator Hitsuji Gondaira is already coming back to the magazine with the start of a new series. Titled Hizuki of the Ginza Patrol , Viz Media has shared the first look at Gondaira's new series ahead of its debut with Shonen Jump this coming weekend. You can check it out below.

Hizuki of the Ginza Patrol will be making its debut with Shonen Jump this weekend, and the first tease for Hitsuji Gondaira's new manga teases it as such, "As the era of the samurai comes to an end, a new type of savior rises!" The synopsis and first look at the new manga sets up a much different kind of series from Mission: Yozakura Family as it's going a more historical setting and tone for its action. Also in comparison, it seems to be presenting one main character to follow rather than a large extended cast at the center of it all.

Hitsuji Gondaira is only one of the experienced Shonen Jump creators returning to the magazine as part of this batch with High School Family: Kokosei Kaizoku' s Ryo Nakama also coming to the magazine this past week. That series had come to take the place of Kenta Shinohara's Witch Watch , and that also means Gondaira's new series is going to slot in the place of the next major series ending with the magazine. So the big changes will be continuing with more endings and more new beginnings.

With the start of Gondaira's new series this weekend, it's also been revealed that Yuto Suzuki's Sakamoto Days is also set to end its run after six long years . This will mark the sixth major series to end with Shonen Jump this year on its own terms, and will mark the 14th title ended with the magazine this year overall when also counting all of the manga that had been cancelled shortly into their runs.
